FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION April 16, 2026 Graduate Council Report 2025-2026-6B At the April 6, 2026 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF BUSINESS Professional Science Masters - PSM, Effective Spring 2027 The Professional Science Masters (PSM) program is a non-thesis graduate degree program that prepares students for leadership and management roles in science- and technology-driven organizations.
Housed in the College of Business, the PSM integrates advanced scientific or technical coursework with professional skills in leadership, project management, communication, and applied problem solving that are broadly applicable in rapidly evolving scientific fields.
This 30–33 credit interdisciplinary degree combines a graduate certificate in a science or technical field with professional business coursework and applied experiential learning.

Students develop practical interpersonal, leadership, communication, and critical thinking skills, and apply these competencies in real-world organizational and industry contexts.
The PSM requires the completion of a graduate certificate in a science field, and four professional courses, including at least one capstone/practicum, and an additional relevant graduate-level course(s) from the URI Online portfolio as elective with Program Director approval.
PSM program tracks that have been certified by the National Professional Science Master's Association should have Industry Advisory Boards and include an integrative, hands-on experiential learning project or applied internship.
The menu of professional courses includes BUS532, BUS506, BUS509, BUS515, MBA540, and BUS557 (MBA557).
Other online courses may be approved by the program director.
At least one 3-credit course must be a capstone/practicum.

If a student does not take BUS515 and the certificate program does not contain a capstone experience, they should take another capstone course from the URI Online portfolio (e.g., PSC592 or MPS598) In addition to the graduate certificate courses, the four professional courses, and the capstone/practicum, students must complete relevant graduate-level course(s) from the URI Online portfolio as electives with Program Director approval (up to 6 credits).

Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design - ABM, Effective Fall 2026 Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design (TMD) Department offers an Accelerated Bachelor of Science to Master of Science Degree in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design (ABMTMD) to allow undergraduates to complete a BS/BA and an MS degree in 5 years.
The program would allow students currently receiving a Bachelor’s of Science in Textiles, Fashion Merchandising and Design; or a Bachelor’s of Science in Textile Marketing; or Bachelor’s degree in any other major combined with a TMD minor Under certain circumstances, students enrolled in programs leading to degrees in related areas may be considered for admission into the TMD program, for example, Business, Chemistry, History, Art History, or Psychology.
In such cases, half of the total credits must be in TMD.
As part of the program, ABMTMD students will need to earn a total of 33 credits (including 11 credits double-counted from their undergraduate degree) Students will also complete industry-oriented capstone project as an independent study (for example, complete an industry-focused case study or an industry-sponsored project).

Finally, students will also successfully complete comprehensive exams on two TMD elective courses.
Courses eligible for double-counting: TMD403 Textile Performance TMD413 Dyeing and Finishing Textiles TMD424 Retail Product Trend Forecasting TMD426 Historic and Contemporary Furniture TMD432 Fashion Retail Supply Chain Management TMD433 Textile Markets TMD434 Branding Fashion Industry TMD440 Historic Textiles TMD441 History of Western Dress TMD442 Fashion Promotion TMD458 Fashion Retail Analytics URI courses outside the TMD Department that are cataloged as eligible for graduate credits can double-count.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCE Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling - MS, Effective Summer 2026 The Master's in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program prepares graduates to work with clients in settings including counseling agencies, hospitals, community mental health centers, and private practice.
Students gain training in evidence-based practice, measurement-based care, develop practical skills in individual and group therapy approaches, as well as career counseling with diverse populations.

This 66-credit program meets curricular requirements for the State of Rhode Island's Licensed Mental Health Counselor (LMHC).
Course Requirements: HDF450, HDF551, HDF570, PSY507, PSY603, PSY615 (3 credits), PSY642, PSY643, PSY644, PSY660, PSY666, PSY670 (18 credits), and PSY672 (12 credits).
A minimum of 66 credits is required to graduate.

This program involves intense clinical practice, including a year-long clinical placement at approved agencies and the department’s Family Therapy Clinic.
A minimum of 60 credits is required for completion of the Couple and Family Therapy pathway within the Human Development and Family Science Program, with an option for 66 credits with thesis. 2) ABM Specialization in Prevention Science Through the Accelerated Bachelor's to Master's (ABM) program, students are able to complete their master’s degree within one year after completion of their Bachelor of Science (B.S) degree.

Through a flexible format where courses are available online, in person, or students can flex between formats, this certificate blends core leadership development with sports-specific business skills.
Students will explore sport as a dynamic venue for social equity, brand-building, revenue generation, and community partnership, while strengthening their capacity to lead diverse teams, shape culture, and drive organizational transformation.

On completion, graduates will be prepared to apply leadership strategies, ethically navigate sport management challenges, and promote inclusive and sustainable sports organizations at the local, national or global level.

We propose a flexible master’s program that offers an attractive path to an interdisciplinary graduate degree to current students in the URI online certificate programs and post-graduate professionals looking to bolster their skill sets and attain higher leadership positions and salaries.
The program would require students to successfully complete a graduate certificate program offered through URI Online, two elective courses, and four professional skills courses.
The mix of professional and discipline-specific skills and knowledge aims to prepare professionals for a broad range of careers across private industry, local, state, federal agencies, and community organizations.
Graduates of the program will be prepared to implement impactful societal, cultural, and economic initiatives.
The program speaks directly to the desire to foster a 21st-century, 24/7 learning environment.
Offered completely online and asynchronously, this program targets working professionals across various disciplines who wish to obtain their credentials while still holding full-time jobs.

The ‘a la carte’ nature of this program highlights the intersection of specialties employers are currently looking for while offering a flexible path to obtaining a master's degree.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and beyond.
This program provides intellectual development for a diverse community of students.
The professional courses and graduate certificates push students to discover the synergies within their certificate areas and business/public administration to foster meaningful and impactful solutions and leadership.
The program integrates online certificate programs offered.
Students completing the certificates are accounted for within their respective programs, so it would not be considered an overlap but rather more of an inclusion.
This proposal describes a PSM framework under which focused tracks will be developed.
There are other master's degree programs that incorporate certificates into the masters (Master's of Public Administration, Masters of Science in Healthcare Management, and proposed Masters of Science in Health Outcomes and Data Analytics).

They are very specific in their focus and audience.
For example, students entering the public administration realm will likely prefer an MPA over this program.
Similarly, students interested in applying data science to healthcare or focusing on healthcare management would likely choose those options.
This program allows for flexibility and broad appeal for students outside of those specific areas of focus.

Master's degrees are steadily growing in popularity as they are increasingly required for mid-to-senior-level positions in many fields.
This program meets the need of many working post-graduates who are seeking master's degrees in professional studies to become more competitive and relevant in the workforce.
The various certificates offered and anticipated through URI Online reflect diverse subject areas.
Accelerated online certificates are attractive to potential students looking to upgrade their skill sets.
This proposed degree supports students achieving an additional credential by offering multiple degree pathways that meet individual student needs within a flexible structure.
Many different tracks can be created in this model. "PSM programs prepare you for science careers in business, government, or nonprofit organizations, where workforce needs are increasing.
Employers of recent PSM graduates in the range from large, multinational pharmaceutical companies to newer biotechnology companies.
Graduates are also working with the federal government or for university technology transfer operations.

Regardless of the employment sector, PSM graduates are finding exciting, well-compensated careers." Source: https://www.professionalsciencemasters.org/about None; the program is intended to be revenue-generating.
Many current students in the URI Online certificate programs have already expressed the desire to obtain a master's degree.
This program allows URI to retain these students by offering them a path to the degree that enhances and augments learning from certificate areas.

Capstone projects will take one of the following forms, depending on availability in a given year: RITIN-affiliated or industry-sponsored projects, in which an external organization presents a real-world problem, and students analyze the issue and propose viable solutions (similar in structure to MBA capstone projects).
These projects will be sourced by graduate faculty advisors, with support from the College’s Professional and Executive Business Education (PEBE) team.
If such projects are not available in a given year, students will complete an industry-focused case study, such as a Harvard-style or Fashion Scholarship Fund (FSF)–inspired case, to be submitted to the department.

Rationale for the proposed restructuring of the ABM–TMD program To increase enrollment in the ABM–TMD program by offering a pathway that better aligns with undergraduate students’ career goals.
To better align the ABM–TMD curriculum with industry needs and expectations.
To provide students with practice-oriented, industry-relevant skills and experiences, rather than a primarily research-oriented academic experience.
Faculty observations indicate that undergraduate students who pursue the accelerated ABM–TMD pathway are primarily motivated by career preparation for the fashion and textile industry.
They seek advanced, applied skills and professional experiences that can directly support their transition into industry roles.

The current research-focused structure of the ABM–TMD program does not fully align with these career goals and, as a result, may limit the program’s appeal and effectiveness for this student population.After the first students went through the program, faculty were of the opinion that a higher threshold was needed for entry into a program designed to be completed in one year.

The current need for mental and behavioral health care in RI is well-documented (i.e., opiate and substance use crises, need for mental health services with emergent needs in child and adolescent mental health).
Furthermore, RI is designated as a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA).
Therefore, there exists an urgent need for master’s level mental and behavioral health clinicians to meet workforce needs in RI and nationally to address these mental health and behavioral health needs.
The Department of Psychology currently has more than 1000 undergraduate majors whose bachelor’s degrees are not sufficient for entry into mental or behavioral health counseling positions.
Students who wish to work in delivery of mental and behavioral services require masters-level training that prepares them for state licensure.

The Psychology Department proposes to develop a professional non-thesis master’s degree in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling at URI to help prepare committed applicants from psychology and related fields for employment opportunities in our field, helping to address the workforce needs of RI employers and, most importantly, supporting the development of these students into an essential resource to meet the critical mental and behavioral health needs of Rhode Islanders.
Graduates of this program will be eligible, with appropriate post-degree supervision hours, for licensure in the state of Rhode Island to become licensed mental health counselors (LMHCs).
These individuals can work in a range of settings (e.g., hospitals, private practice, community mental health centers) and, when licensed, provide services that can be reimbursed by all major insurance providers.
The Psychology Department has a 50-year history of applied graduate programs in Clinical (PhD) and historically School (master’s and PhD) focus areas.
Our PhD program in Clinical Psychology has been fully accredited by the American Psychological Association since 1972.

It is expected that a new professional Master's degree program will easily fit into pre- existing resources and structures: 1) our existing graduate curriculum for our Clinical PhD program currently meets the Discipline-Specific Knowledge, Profession-Wide Competencies, and Learning/Curriculum Elements required by the American Psychological Association for Master’s degree program accreditation, 2) faculty and staff are already teaching the majority of the required courses (didactic and experiential supervisory training), as well as 3) the Psychology Department has an in- house training clinic, the Psychological Consultation Center, that is directed by a full-time PhD clinical psychologist and is a principal training site for current doctoral students.
Psychology’s Master’s Program in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling proposed here aligns with several elements of the URI’s Strategic Plan including: 1.
Strategic Priority 1; Broadening URI’s Impact - Goal 1.

This program is designed to contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation and beyond – by increasing the number of Master’s-trained license-eligible well prepared mental health professionals added to the RI and regional workforce to address pressing mental and behavioral health needs. 2.
Strategic Priority 2; Enhance Student Achievement- Goal 2: This new master’s program at URI will be a career preparation track that will be attractive to Psychology’s large pool of undergraduate majors as well as to regional applicants.
The significant need for well-trained license-eligible master’s students in RI, regionally, and nationally is likely to continue given mental illness upward trends. 3.

Strategic Priority 3; Foster an Inclusive Culture - Goal 2: This new master’s program will continue the Psychology Departments deep commitment to and significant ongoing efforts (e.g., standing departmental Inclusion and Diversity Committee) to build an innovative, contemporary, and professional learning environment and workplace that values diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility with leadership that is principle-centered and effective. 4.
Strategic Priority 4; Power the University of the Future - Goals 3 & 4: This new master’s program will help URI secure the necessary resources to sustain and grow the university and will generate a new revenue stream for years to come.

URI has the potential to be a major player in addressing our state’s mental health workforce needs as well as helping to address the national mental health crisis.
There would be modest overlap with the Master of Science program in the Human Development and Family Science department insofar as both Programs would lead to licensure at the Master's level.
However, the HDF program's graduates are eligible only to be licensed as Marriage and Family Therapists (LMFTs) whereas the graduates of the Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling will be eligible only to be licensed as Mental Health Counselors (LMHCs).
Although the two programs provide training in counseling and use external placements for their training, the two programs differ in terms of the requirements for licensure of the supervisors providing the training (students in the HDF Master's require supervisors to be LMFTs; students in the Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will have supervisors who are LMHC, MSWs, or PhDs).
The two programs are working together to share resources to the benefit of both programs (e.g., students in each program will be required to take class(es) in the other program).

The Masters in Mental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will also overlap with the Clinical Psychology doctoral program; yet, we see this as tremendously advantageous to both programs.
Many courses in the Doctoral program will be shared with the Masters program ensuring fully enrolled classes that run each year (currently, several classes in the clinical program run every other year due to low enrollments).
In addition, the doctoral program has an excess of clinical externship sites requesting students for training.
The new Master's program would help to meet this demand and offer training opportunities to students in placements that have long-standing training collaborations with the doctoral program.
Finally, the Masters program will offer courses (e.g., Group Counseling) that students in the doctoral program may wish to take.

Fall 2026 Existing No Date Chosen Spring 2027 Existing No Date Chosen Changes Rationale for Proposed Changes We are changing the description for our Master of Science in Human Development and Family Science to reflect our newly designed and approved ABM program in HDF with a specialization in Prevention Science.
The previous description and admission requirements were reflective of our former Master of Science Specializing in Developmental Science program that no longer exists.
In addition, we propose allowing two options to complete the Couple and Family Therapy specialization: the capstone option (already approved) and the thesis option (a new option).
For those in the capstone option, there are no changes as the capstone is completed in HDF 581 in the final semester which is already a part of the program.
For those wanting to complete a thesis, we propose allowing the student to complete the thesis upon enrolling in and successfully completing a minimum 6 credits of HDF 599 and a successful thesis defense.
We propose this to be fully optional for each student enrolled in the CFT specialization.

For students who select this graduation pathway, they would be required to take additional coursework (HDF 599); although in some cases, some of these credits could overlap with student electives.
We anticipate students would take 60 credits (existing requirement for all students) in the capstone option; those who select the thesis option would take between 63-66 credits depending on their elective choices.
These changes are reflected in the specialization-level proposal for CFT.

Admission requirements: GPA of 3.2 or higher, 18 undergraduate credits from relevant disciplines, including human development and family studies/science, psychology, and sociology.
Majors in related fields (e.g., nursing, political science, education) may be admitted with the permission of the director of graduate studies.
Completion of an undergraduate level statistics course taken either prior to the beginning of the program or during the first year of the program is required.
Two letters of recommendation are required with at least one from an academic reference.
Application deadline for fall admission is February 15.
Applications received after that date will be reviewed on a space-available basis, with April 1st as the final deadline for applications.
Program requirements: a minimum of 36 credits of approved graduate courses that include: a) developmental seminars, b) courses in policy and research, c) a professional seminar, and d) the completion of a master’s thesis.

Additionally, students have the option of including up to 3 credits of a policy, administrative, or research internship as part of the program of study.
Master of Science Specializing in Couple and Family Therapy Admission requirements: GPA 3.3 or higher recommended.
At least 9 credits of relevant preparation, including courses in family relations, developmental theory, and introduction to counseling or equivalent courses.
Two letters of recommendation should be from supervisors/faculty in a related field attesting to observed experience, emotional stability, and maturity.
After initial screening, qualified applicants will be required to come to campus for a personal interview.
